summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted API for chat/text generation focused on rate control, streaming quirks, retry/backoff best practices, and fallback patterns to cheaper model variants. Customer (Cobalt) is evaluating for a user-facing analytics chat assistant with a Q1 pilot. Key asks: predictable 95th latency under load, data residency/SOC2 notes, pricing buckets and a bench run on their prompt set.
topics: Generation params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop sequences)
Redwood Console: per-route quotas and telemetry
Optimize suggestions: batching, KV caching, quantization recommendations
transcript:
[00:00] Michael Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Michael, account lead at Redwood Inference. With me is Sara, our solutions engineer. Quick intro then we'll jump into a short hosted API demo focused on rate controls and fallback patterns.
[00:15] Rajiv Menon: Hi Michael, thanks. Quick context — we're building an analytics chat assistant embedded in our dashboard, expecting ~50k monthly active users in pilot, Q1 timeline. Main concerns are cost and latency at 95th percentile.
[00:30] Sara Patel: Great, thanks Rajiv. We'll demo the streaming response behavior and show how you can gate tokens, use early-stop, and route to a cheaper model variant on overload.
[01:05] Tom Leary: Quick question upfront, do you support server-side retries or do we have to implement retries client-side?
[01:20] Sara Patel: We recommend client-side retries with server-assisted guidance. Redwood returns clear status codes for transient capacity errors and we expose a Retry-After header. The typical pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, cap at 3 attempts, and fall back to a smaller model or a cached response on failure.
[01:55] Elena Ruiz: Are streaming responses resumable mid-kv-cache? We use long conversations with KV cache to avoid recomputing system prompts.
[02:10] Sara Patel: Great question. The runtime manages a KV cache (sometimes transcribed as K V cash in auto transcripts), and streaming is tied to the request's generation window. We don't reattach to partial streams; instead we return chunked deltas. For resumed context you send the kv cache id + prefix tokens and the model picks up. There can be small differences depending on quantization mode.
[03:00] Michael Chen: I'm going to share my screen — quick curl examples from hosted API. Note: link to docs in chat - https://redwood.ai/docs/hosted-api (mock).
[03:30] Sara Patel: Example 1 — streaming chat with temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9. We show a live stream where you start seeing the assistant token-by-token. Important operational note: streaming reduces tail latency for perceived time-to-first-byte but does not reduce total compute cost; so for low-cost use cases, consider a smaller model or shorter max_tokens.
[04:20] Rajiv Menon: On retries: if we do 3 retries with exponential backoff, what's the recommended base? 200ms? 500ms?
[04:35] Sara Patel: We typically recommend base 250ms with factor 2 and jitter, but tune to your SLA. For user-facing chat we do a shorter base to keep interactive feel. The Console can surface average retry counts per route so you can monitor cost impact.
[05:00] Speaker 4: (inaudible) — is there a way to do circuit breaker style so we stop retrying after a certain global error budget?
[05:15] Sara Patel: Yes — implement a local circuit breaker and Redwood can emit capacity error metrics to CloudWatch/Datadog. In Console you can set per-route rate limits & circuit-break thresholds that return specific error codes, which your client can use to trigger fallback logic.
[06:10] Tom Leary: For the fallback, do you route to a different API key/model or does Redwood do that automatically?
[06:25] Michael Chen: You can configure routing policies in the Console — e.g., prefer hosted-xlarge, fallback to hosted-small when latency exceeds SLO or capacity is low. Redwood also supports a policy to route cross-region or to Dedicated if you have that contract. We'll show the routing policy UI in a sec.
[07:00] Sara Patel: Demo: switching model in response to higher latency. Watch the request ID here — first request goes to rwd-xl, second route policy kicks in and routes to rwd-medium. Notice the cost delta in the response metadata.
[07:40] Elena Ruiz: Is that cost metadata returned on every call? We need per-call cost for chargeback to product teams.
[07:55] Sara Patel: Yes, we return a token-level cost estimate in response metadata when enabled. Console also has token-cost breakdowns by model and route.
[09:00] Rajiv Menon: Security — we have to ensure PII never leaves our VPC. Hosted won't work unless we can encrypt and provide a key?
[09:20] Michael Chen: For PII/PHI we often recommend Redwood Private (VPC) or Dedicated with VPC peering. For hosted we offer mTLS, field-level encryption, and optional customer-managed KMS for key wrapping on stored artifacts like logs. We'll send SOC2 docs and a KMS integration guide after the call.
[10:05] Speaker 4: (overlap) what's the retention on logs in hosted?
[10:15] Sara Patel: Default is 30 days but you can change retention in Console. For customers with compliance needs we can redact or opt-out of storing generation text. We'll attach the retention configurator link in the follow-up.
[11:00] Sara Patel: Now a quick look at failure modes — capacity error (HTTP 429), model-unavailable (503-ish), and transient kernel OOMs which sometimes surface as 500 with a short Retry-After. For each we recommend a specific client behavior: 429 -> exponential backoff and retry; 503 -> quick fallback to smaller model; 500 kernel OOM -> send to a fallback queue and alert SRE.
[12:20] Tom Leary: If we fall back to a smaller model, how do we ensure response quality doesn't collapse? We have strict UX standards.
[12:35] Sara Patel: Two options: 1) use a cascade pre-warm policy where you keep a tiny hot pool of cheaper models for short lat spikes; 2) send a condensed prompt to the smaller model (e.g., compress long context into summary) so quality degrades gracefully. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles to keep quality while reducing cost.
[13:50] Rajiv Menon: Can you show the Console rule for routing?
[14:05] Michael Chen: Sure — switching to Console view: per-route rules allow thresholds by 95p latency, token burn, or error rate. You can set action to 'route to variant', 'throttle', or 'serve cached response'.
[15:00] Sara Patel: Note: cached prefix/KV caching works best for high-reuse prompts. If your users ask repetitive queries, the automatic prefix cache will hit and reduce compute. There's a small config to tune TTL and cache key strategy.
[16:30] Elena Ruiz: Any tips for setting max_tokens properly? We saw models sometimes over-generate and blow past our token budget.
[16:50] Sara Patel: Use stop sequences plus a hard max_tokens. Also set a content policy: if response length could vary a lot, compute expected token bounds on the client and set a conservative max_tokens. For interactive assistant use-case we default to 150-250 for short answers.
[18:00] Michael Chen: Quick architecture suggestion for your pilot: start hosted with a reserved burst capacity and a routing policy that can escalate to Dedicated if traffic grows. That gives you predictable baseline and low friction onboarding.
[19:15] Rajiv Menon: Cost question — can you give a rough per-1000 message estimate for rwd-xl vs rwd-medium?
[19:30] Michael Chen: Ballpark: rwd-xl ~ $12/1k messages (depends on tokens), rwd-medium ~ $3.5/1k. We'll send a cost worksheet that calculates per-token vs per-generation.
[20:10] Speaker 4: (mumble) — you mentioned Optimize. How does Optimize recommend quantization?
[20:25] Sara Patel: Optimize runs pattern analysis on your prompt set and suggests per-route quantization or batching thresholds. It will recommend aggressive int8 quant for non-critical routes and int4 for high-throughput internal pipelines. We also attach a quality delta estimate.
[21:45] Elena Ruiz: For benching, do you have a tool to replay our real prompt logs?
[21:58] Sara Patel: Yes — we have a small runner that replays logged prompts with preserved timing to a sandbox project. We'll run that on your dataset; that's actually the bench we're proposing.
[23:00] Michael Chen: Quick demo of retry jitter: see this client snippet — adds +/- 100ms jitter to avoid thundering herd. Important when you have many clients re-try simultaneously.
[24:10] Rajiv Menon: How do you surface throttled requests in Console? We need visibility when clients are being rate-limited to tune quotas.
[24:30] Sara Patel: Console has per-route metrics showing throttle count, average retry latency, and token burn. You can also set alerts for throttle thresholds.
[25:00] Tom Leary: Do you support function/tool-calling in the hosted API? We might want structured outputs.
[25:15] Sara Patel: Yes — function-calling and structured JSON outputs are supported. We can show how to use typed schema and partial streaming of function arguments. Note: streaming structured outputs can be tricky if the client expects atomic JSON — use a finalization step to validate.
[26:30] Elena Ruiz: Any gotchas with streaming and web-sockets vs HTTP server-sent events?
[26:45] Sara Patel: SSE is simpler for browser clients, WebSocket is lower latency for persistent connections. Both supported. However, SSE imposes some limits in older proxies — we recommend pinned keepalives and testing in your infra.
[28:00] Michael Chen: We're going to run a quick end-to-end: client issues chat request -> streamed tokens -> simulated capacity spike -> automatic fallback to smaller model. Watch the response id and cost meta.
[29:10] Speaker 4: (crosstalk) — the fallback looked slightly cut-off, was that due to max_tokens?
[29:25] Sara Patel: Yep, smaller model had shorter max_tokens setting; we truncated to keep latency acceptable. You can configure consistent max_tokens across variants if you want to preserve length.
[31:00] Rajiv Menon: For SOC2 and audits, do you provide logs that indicate who requested what? We need immutable audit logs for compliance.
[31:20] Michael Chen: Yes — audit log exports include request id, api key id, route, timestamps, and redacted payloads if you choose. We can integrate with your SIEM via secure forwarding.
[32:15] Elena Ruiz: Does Redwood expose per-token billing in the response? We want to map cost back to product features.
[32:30] Sara Patel: Yes — response meta gives token counts and cost estimate; Console provides aggregated reports and cost by tag/route. You can also use token attribution hooks in SDKs to label usage.
[33:40] Michael Chen: Let's talk timelines. If you want to pilot in mid-Jan we recommend: sign up sandbox by end of Dec, run bench, then 2-week pilot with canary routing.
[34:05] Rajiv Menon: That aligns. We need an internal procurement approval — who should be on the legal/procurement thread?
[34:20] Michael Chen: I'll loop in our legal ops; Sara will share the enterprise checklist. For privacy-sensitive items we can include our compliance packet.
[35:10] Speaker 4: Small note — we use Okta SAML. Any pre-reqs?
[35:25] Sara Patel: SSO via SAML/Okta is supported. We'll send the metadata file and example mappings.
[36:15] Elena Ruiz: If we start with hosted and later want to move to Dedicated, how disruptive is the migration?
[36:30] Sara Patel: Minimal from API perspective — same endpoints and SDKs. We assist with model pinning and traffic split to make rollouts safe. Data residency and key management may need extra steps.
[37:40] Michael Chen: Quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing + quota sheet, the bench run plan, SOC2 and KMS docs, and propose security deep-dive for 12/29. Sara will run the bench.
[38:10] Rajiv Menon: Sounds good. One last thing — can we get a sample SLA for latency?
[38:25] Michael Chen: Yes, for Dedicated we can provide SLOs. Hosted provides best-effort with burst guarantees depending on reserved capacity. We'll include a sample SLA in follow-up.
[39:00] Tom Leary: Thanks — useful session.
[39:10] Speaker 4: Thanks all.
[41:00] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts. End call.
[41:30] (end recording)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings (K V cash vs KV cache, Sam'l vs SAML), some crosstalk. The demo included a brief shared screen curl snippet and Console UI that are referenced by links in follow-up.
